speakers: Bob Stine (Department of Statistics, Wharton, University of Pennsylvania)
summary: Question: how to judge and size investments statistically. Method: dice simulation for volatility drag and Kelly sizing; CAPM regressions of Exxon, Berkshire, 'Bob', 'TEAM' (monthly 1980-2009); martingale (CERT) test of alpha via Doob's inequality plus Bonferroni. Conclusion: t-tests flag all four alphas, the robust martingale test only Berkshire, and multiplicity weakens even that.

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Convincing going forward?
claims.claim: Growth of $1 from 1980 differs hugely across Exxon, Berkshire, 'Bob' and 'TEAM', but a cumulative-value chart alone does not show whether that performance will persist.
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate
claims.reported_result: Chart (log scale) $1 in 1980 to ~2009: Berkshire ~$55 (peak ~$85 in 2008), Exxon ~$15, Bob ~$6.5, TEAM ~$1.5 (read from image)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Guarantees 2% excess annual returns above any benchmark you want. Guaranteed.
claims.claim: A fund promising a steady 2% annual excess return over any benchmark is set up as a puzzle: such smooth outperformance can be manufactured by hidden tail risk (resolved on slide 44).

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Focus on returns, not cumulative value or prices
claims.claim: Evaluating investments should use returns rather than cumulative value, because one good year does not imply continuing success.

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Remove market performance (CAPM)
claims.claim: Market exposure should be removed with a CAPM regression before judging skill; leverage on the market looked like skill until the recent crash.
claims.exact_rule: Judge skill by alpha from regression of excess returns on market excess returns
claims.conditions: leverage made funds look good until 2008

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Watch for unseen volatility (Peso problem)
claims.claim: Strategies can carry risks not yet seen in the sample (peso problem): absence of a loss does not mean a loss is impossible.

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Adjust for multiplicity
claims.claim: Significance must be adjusted for the number of investments considered (multiple testing).

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Data: Yahoo finance, Jan 1950 - Feb 2009, 710 months
claims.claim: A dollar in the S&P 500 from January 1950 grew at roughly 7% a year, appearing as a near straight line on a log scale.
claims.reported_result: ~7% annual growth, Jan 1950-Feb 2009, 710 months; $1 grows to roughly $50-90 (chart, log and linear scale)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Too easy to be deceived...
claims.claim: Cumulative value charts deceive: a 'Special' series looks dramatically better than the market even though the difference may be a small per-period edge compounded, so one should compare returns.
claims.reported_result: Chart 1950-2009: 'Special' peaks ~180 vs market ~90 and ends ~97 vs ~50 (read from image)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Much simpler structure, almost iid...
claims.claim: Monthly S&P 500 returns have a much simpler, almost iid structure than prices, punctuated by crashes such as Oct 1987, Aug 1998 and Oct 2008.
claims.reported_result: Monthly returns roughly between -0.22 and +0.15, 1950-2009; marked outliers Oct 1987 'Black Monday', Aug 1998 LTCM, Oct 2008 banking crisis

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.claim: Monthly S&P 500 returns average 0.64% with SD 4.15%; their distribution has fat tails relative to the normal.
claims.reported_result: Monthly 1950-2009: mean 0.0064, s 0.0415, s^2 0.0017; normal quantile plot shows fat left and right tails
claims.exhibit: Slide 9 histogram and normal quantile plot

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Fat tails more apparent in daily data.
claims.claim: Fat tails are more pronounced in daily returns (mean 0.03%, SD 0.95%).

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Sequence of “bets” that appear nearly independent, but correlation remains between assets.
claims.claim: Asset returns behave like a sequence of nearly independent bets over time, but they are correlated with each other; risk is the variation in returns.
claims.exact_rule: R_t = (P_t - P_{t-1})/P_{t-1}; risk = SD of R_t

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Trade off return for risk?
claims.claim: Over 1980-2009 the higher-mean assets also had higher monthly volatility, raising the question of how to trade return for risk.
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Start with the whole-market index
claims.claim: Investing involves two questions, how much wealth to commit and which assets; the answer to 'which' starts with the whole-market index and then asks what to add.
claims.exact_rule: Core holding = whole-market index; add other assets only if they improve on it

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: How do you decide: risk versus return?
claims.claim: Three hypothetical investments differ sharply in mean and SD (Green 7.5%/20%, Red 71%/132%, White 0%/6%), posing how to weigh risk against return.
claims.reported_result: Annual mean/SD: Green 7.5%/20%; Red 71%/132%; White 0%/6%

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: “Being Warren Buffett”, Amer Statistician, 2006
claims.claim: In the dice game each round multiplies wealth by a die outcome: Green 0.8/0.9/1.05/1.1/1.2/1.4, Red 0.06/0.2/1/3/3/3, White 0.9/1/1/1/1/1.1; the setup comes from the author's 'Being Warren Buffett' (American Statistician, 2006).

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Red is “exciting” but generally loses value.
claims.claim: In typical simulations Red swings wildly and ends near zero, Green (calibrated to US stock-market excess returns) grows steadily, and White (calibrated to T-bills) goes nowhere.
claims.reported_result: Typical run over 20 rounds from 1000: Green ~10,000-12,000, White ~1,000, Red ~0 after peaks near 4,900 (read from image)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: In 20 rounds, the expected value of Red is
claims.claim: Red's expected value after 20 rounds is 1.71^20, about 45,700 times the start, and occasionally a run soars, yet this is driven by rare paths.
claims.reported_result: E[Red after 20 rounds] = 1.71^20 = 45,700 x initial; occasional run reaches ~10^8 from 1000 by round 12 (chart, log scale)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: In the long run, Red will lose (w.p. 1)
claims.claim: Although Red has a huge expected value, almost every path loses most of its value and in the long run Red loses with probability one; the few lucky winners look like 'Warren Buffetts'.
claims.direction: avoid assets with negative long-run growth even if mean is high

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: How can I recognize that Red will lose without waiting for it to happen?
claims.claim: The practical question is how to recognise a long-run loser in advance and how to exploit it anyway.

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: If the r t are independent over time, then
claims.claim: With independent returns, long-run wealth grows at about E(r) - Var(r)/2 per period (volatility drag), so Green grows (0.055), while Red (-0.16) and White (-0.002) shrink.
claims.exact_rule: W_t = W_0 prod(1+r_i) ~ W_0 (1 + E(r) - Var(r)/2)^t; long-run growth g = E(r) - Var(r)/2

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Mix investments rather than leaving everything in one.
claims.claim: A 50/50 mix of Red and White (Pink) halves the mean but cuts variance by four, giving positive long-run growth of 0.14 even though neither asset grows alone.
claims.exact_rule: Pink = 0.5 Red + 0.5 White, rebalanced each round; E = 0.355, Var = 0.435, g = E - Var/2 = 0.14
claims.reported_result: E(Pink) = 0.355; Var(Pink) = 0.435; long-run growth 0.14
claims.conditions: assets independent; weights rebalanced every period

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Over short horizons, a poor long-term investment might appear very attractive.
claims.claim: Long-run return is E - Var/2, so short samples can make a poor long-run investment look attractive, and portfolios succeed by trading expected return for lower variance.
claims.exact_rule: long-run return = E(return) - 0.5 Var(return)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Real investments lack some properties of the investments in the dice simulation
claims.claim: Unlike the dice, real investments are not independent of each other, their properties change over time, and their parameters are unknown.
claims.conditions: dependence, instability and estimation error weaken the dice lessons

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Long run Return
claims.claim: On 1980-2009 monthly data the long-run (volatility-adjusted) return ranks Berkshire first, then Exxon, Bob and TEAM.
claims.exact_rule: long-run return = mean - SD^2/2 (monthly)
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: If we accept the objective to maximize long- run wealth, then the proportion of our wealth p to put in an investment is
claims.claim: To maximise long-run wealth the fraction of wealth to put in an asset is p = (mu - rf) / sigma^2 (Kelly rule).
claims.exact_rule: p = (mu - r_f) / sigma^2 (fraction of wealth; >1 means leverage; <0 means short)
claims.data_needed: expected excess return and variance of the asset

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: μ and σ for the entire history of the market
claims.claim: Using the whole market history this rule says to hold about 1.75 times wealth in stocks, which the dice example suggests is more than people's risk aversion would accept.
claims.reported_result: p = 0.075/0.040 = 1.75 times wealth (as printed; 0.075/0.040 equals 1.875)
claims.indicator: US stock market excess return and variance

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Nonetheless, we ought to invest some fraction of our wealth in any asset for which we know μ ≠ 0 (short it if μ < 0).
claims.claim: Any asset with a known non-zero expected excess return deserves some position, long if positive and short if negative.
claims.exact_rule: position sign = sign(mu - r_f); size per Kelly rule
claims.direction: long if mu>0, short if mu<0
claims.conditions: mu must be known, not just estimated

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Messy problem of portfolio analysis is to anticipate correlations going forward.
claims.claim: With many correlated assets, sizing each in isolation is wrong; the hard part of portfolio analysis is forecasting correlations.

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Invest first in the market as a whole
claims.claim: Finance theory says to hold the whole market first and then consider other assets.
claims.exact_rule: Hold market portfolio; evaluate other assets relative to it (alpha)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Regress growth in current year on prior growth
claims.claim: A regression of 1,500 mutual funds' 1993 returns on their 1992 returns is 'statistically significant' (negative), but the sign changes in other years, because the 1,500 observations are dependent, not independent.
claims.reported_result: Return93 = 18.63 (SE 0.468, t 39.83) - 0.491 x Return92 (SE 0.0424, t -11.57); sign changes in other years (slide 28 table)
claims.conditions: cross-sectional dependence (common market moves) inflates t-statistics

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Explanation: 1,500 dependent observations...
claims.claim: Cross-sectional dependence among funds (common shocks) makes naive t-statistics wildly overstated, so apparent persistence or reversal is unreliable.

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Plot average return on SD of return for a collection of randomly formed portfolios
claims.claim: Among randomly formed portfolios, mixing the tangent (market) portfolio with lending or borrowing at the risk-free rate gives better risk-return than any other portfolio.
claims.exact_rule: Hold tangent portfolio; lend (below) or borrow (above) at r_f to reach desired risk
claims.reported_result: Chart: r_f ~0.01; tangent portfolio at SD ~0.10, return ~0.037; random portfolios SD 0.05-0.27, returns -0.05 to +0.06 (read from image)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Excess returns on an asset are related to those on whole market by a linear equation
claims.claim: Excess asset returns are regressed on market excess returns, R_t - r_f = alpha + beta (M_t - r_f) + e_t; CAPM says alpha = 0 and specific returns are uncorrelated with the market.
claims.exact_rule: OLS: R_t - r_f = alpha + beta (M_t - r_f) + e_t; beta = Cov(R-r_f, M-r_f)/Var(M-r_f); specific return w_t = (R_t-r_f) - beta (M_t-r_f)
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Intrinsic variation in asset has non-zero mean
claims.claim: If alpha is not zero, the asset's specific return has a non-zero mean and one should buy (or sell) some amount of it on top of the market.
claims.exact_rule: If alpha>0 add long position; if alpha<0 short; size by Kelly on specific return
claims.direction: long if alpha>0, short if alpha<0

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: All have substantial correlation with the returns on the whole market (market risk)
claims.claim: All four investments load substantially on the market; Exxon shows monthly alpha 0.006 (t 2.68) and Berkshire 0.01 (t 3.12) in simple CAPM regressions.
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate
claims.reported_result: CAPM scatter 1980-2009 monthly: Exxon alpha 0.006 t 2.68; Berkshire alpha 0.01 t 3.12; Bob and TEAM lie almost on the regression line (read from image)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Residuals often deviate from the usual assumptions of simple regression.
claims.claim: CAPM residuals often violate regression assumptions: Bob's residuals take two distinct levels and TEAM's fan out in an X pattern against the market, indicating non-normal, non-linear behaviour.
claims.reported_result: Residual plots vs excess.vw: Exxon/Berkshire diffuse; Bob residuals mostly ~-0.001 with a cluster at ~+0.015; TEAM residuals X-shaped, range ~-0.02 to +0.03 (read from image)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Standard procedure relies on t-distribution to obtain p-value
claims.claim: The usual test of H0: alpha = 0 regresses out the market and uses a t-distribution; for Exxon this gives alpha 0.0062 (t 2.68, p 0.0077) and beta 0.56.
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Do you believe these results?
claims.claim: Standard t-tests say all four alphas are significant, including a tiny Bob alpha with t 5.5, which the author invites the audience to doubt.
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Some investments produce returns that are far from Gaussian, with large outliers (fat tails)
claims.claim: The t-statistic's distribution is doubtful because some returns are far from Gaussian with fat tails, CAPM residuals are dependent, and volatility clusters (ARCH).

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Nonetheless want a p-value
claims.claim: Despite model risk, an investor still needs a valid p-value for alpha.

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Assume only that E(w t |w t-1 ,w t-2 ,…) = 0 (not nec. iid)
claims.claim: The martingale test (CERT) assumes only that specific returns have zero conditional mean under the null, not iid or normality.
claims.exact_rule: w_t = (R_t - r_f) - beta (M_t - r_f); H0: E(w_t | past) = 0

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: CERT p-value from Doob’s inequality
claims.claim: Under the null, compound specific returns C_t = prod(1+w_i) are a non-negative martingale, so Doob's inequality gives P(max C_t >= gamma) <= 1/gamma; the p-value is 1/max C_t.
claims.exact_rule: C_t = prod_{i<=t}(1+w_i); p-value = 1 / max_{t<=n} C_t (Doob: P(max C >= gamma) <= 1/gamma)
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: To reject H 0 at 0.05 level, compound returns have to exceed 20 during observed period
claims.claim: To reject no-alpha at the 5% level, the compounded market-neutral (specific) return must exceed 20 times its start at some point in the sample, a far tougher bar than a t-test.
claims.exact_rule: Reject H0 at level a if max_t C_t >= 1/a (=20 for a=0.05)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Since the martingale test does not depend on n, we can use finely spaced data that essentially reveal β (if you believe it’s fixed!)
claims.claim: Because the martingale test's bound does not depend on sample size, beta can be estimated precisely from high-frequency data, provided beta is constant.
claims.exact_rule: Estimate beta b on fine (e.g. daily) data; compute residual returns (R_t - r_f) - b (M_t - r_f)
claims.conditions: beta assumed fixed over the sample

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: “Residual” returns for Exxon,
claims.claim: Exxon's compounded residual (CERT) return rose from 1 in 1980 to a peak near 7.8 in 2008, well short of the 20 needed to reject at 5%.
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate
claims.reported_result: Exxon CERT returns 1980-2009: ~1 to ~2 by 1990, ~3.5 by 2000, peak ~7.8 in 2008, ~6.5 end (read from image)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Only Berkshire Hathaway rejects the null, and then we have to consider multiplicity.
claims.claim: With the martingale test only Berkshire Hathaway's compounded residual return exceeds 20, so only it rejects zero alpha, and even that must survive a multiplicity adjustment; Exxon, Bob and TEAM fail.
claims.data_needed: monthly total returns 1980-2009 for Exxon, Berkshire Hathaway, 'Bob', 'TEAM'; CRSP value-weighted market (excess.vw); T-bill rate
claims.reported_result: CERT 1980-2009: Berkshire crosses 20 around 1998 and peaks ~26 in 2008; Exxon max ~7.8; Bob rises steadily to ~1.75; TEAM max ~1.35 (read from image)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Multiply the p-value from martingale test by number of assets considered.
claims.claim: A martingale p-value of 1/20 does not survive multiple testing; the Bonferroni fix multiplies it by the number of assets considered, which is usually more than four.
claims.exact_rule: Adjusted p = min(1, m / max C_t) where m = number of assets/strategies considered

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: The test is “tight” in the sense that there are processes you would not want to consider for which it gets the right answer,
claims.claim: The martingale test is tight: there exist processes (like the Bob Fund) for which its bound is exact, so it cannot be made more powerful without assumptions.

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: How do you guarantee those 2% above benchmark returns?
claims.claim: The 'Bob Fund' delivers smooth excess returns by earning 1/k each period with probability k/(k+1) and losing everything with probability 1/(k+1), so its expected excess return is zero; with k=19 it shows a bit over 2% growth until it busts.
claims.exact_rule: r_t = 1/k w.p. k/(k+1); r_t = -1 w.p. 1/(k+1); E(r_t) = 0; example k = 19
claims.direction: smooth positive excess returns hide a rare total loss
claims.conditions: looks good until the rare loss happens (peso problem)

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Martingale test protects against the “until it happens” unobserved volatility
claims.claim: For any k, the chance that the Bob Fund's compounded excess return ever exceeds 20 is exactly 1/20, so the martingale test keeps its stated size even against hidden-tail-risk strategies.
claims.reported_result: P(C_t of Bob Fund > 20) = 1/20 for any k

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Watch for unseen volatility using robust test
claims.claim: The recommended workflow is: use returns, regress out the market (CAPM), test alpha with the martingale (CERT) test robust to hidden volatility, and adjust for multiplicity with Bonferroni.
claims.exact_rule: returns -> CAPM residuals -> CERT p = 1/max C_t -> Bonferroni x number of candidates

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Bonferroni does fine, particularly since it’s hard to “count” the considered alternatives
claims.claim: Bonferroni is adequate because the true number of alternatives considered is hard to count anyway.

claims.speaker: Bob Stine
claims.quote: Foster, Stine, Young (2008) “A martingale test for alpha”
claims.claim: The test is from Foster, Stine and Young (2008), 'A martingale test for alpha'.
claims.testable: partly - paper not in this deck

reasoning.question: How should an investor judge whether an investment's past outperformance reflects genuine skill (alpha) that will persist, and how much to invest in it, when returns are fat-tailed, dependent, and many candidates are examined?

thesis.statement: Judge investments on returns, not cumulative value; size by long-run growth (E - Var/2, Kelly); remove market exposure with CAPM; and test alpha with a martingale (CERT) test that needs compounded residual returns to exceed 1/alpha (20 at 5%), adjusted by Bonferroni for the number of candidates. On this test only Berkshire's 1980-2009 alpha survives, and even it is marginal after multiplicity.

foundations.premise: Returns over time are nearly independent (close to iid), though correlated across assets.
Returns are fat-tailed, especially at daily frequency, and CAPM residuals are non-Gaussian and dependent (ARCH).
Long-run wealth compounds, so the relevant return is the geometric (E - Var/2), not the arithmetic mean.
The market portfolio is the tangent portfolio; skill is only what remains after removing market exposure.
Strategies can hide rare large losses (peso problem) that a finite sample never shows.
Investors search over many candidates, so the best observed alpha is inflated (multiplicity).

mechanism_chain.to: low or negative long-run growth despite high mean

mechanism_chain.why: variance falls faster than mean (by 4 vs 2 for a 50/50 mix)
maximising E - Var/2 over the fraction invested

mechanism_chain.to: specific return after removing market beta
mechanism_chain.why: market exposure is available cheaply via the index

mechanism_chain.from: specific returns with zero conditional mean (no alpha)
mechanism_chain.to: compounded specific return is a non-negative martingale
valid p-value 1/max C_t regardless of tails or dependence

mechanism_chain.why: Bonferroni multiply by number of candidates

design_rationale.choice: Use returns rather than cumulative value/prices
design_rationale.reason_given: cumulative charts deceive; returns are close to iid

design_rationale.sensitivity: market history gives 1.75x leverage, which the author considers too aggressive

design_rationale.choice: CAPM regression to remove market risk
design_rationale.reason_given: market can be bought directly; leverage looked like skill
t-test unreliable with fat tails, dependence, ARCH; CERT assumes only zero conditional mean
design_rationale.sensitivity: t-test rejects for all four; CERT only for Berkshire

design_rationale.choice: Estimate beta from finely spaced data
design_rationale.reason_given: CERT bound does not depend on n
simple; number of alternatives is hard to count anyway

evidence_map.result: Dice game: Red (mean 71%) loses almost surely; 50/50 Red/White mix grows at 0.14
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) real assets are correlated and parameters unknown, as the author notes

evidence_map.result: t-tests find significant alpha for Exxon, Berkshire, Bob and (negative) TEAM; CERT rejects only for Berkshire

evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) Berkshire's alpha may be a factor exposure (value, quality, low-beta) or survivorship-selected; after Bonferroni over many candidates it may also fail

evidence_map.result: Bob Fund with hidden total-loss risk exceeds 20 with probability exactly 1/20
evidence_map.tests: step 6: test keeps size against peso-type strategies
evidence_map.rules_out: smooth-return strategies passing at a rate above test size
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) low power for genuine small alphas over short samples

evidence_map.result: Mutual fund 1993-on-1992 slope -0.49, t -11.6, but sign flips across years

evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) genuine time-varying reversal from style rotation

regimes.effect: leveraged market exposure looks like skill until a crash
outliers dominate tails; peso-type risks materialise
a poor long-run investment can look very attractive

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Kelly example prints p = 0.075/0.040 = 1.75; the arithmetic gives 1.875
Identity and construction of 'Bob' and 'TEAM' series are not explained on the slides
Market proxy (excess.vw), risk-free series and beta-estimation frequency for the CERT results are not fully stated
Power of the martingale test (how large/long an alpha is needed to reach 20) is not quantified
CERT assumes constant beta; time-varying beta would leak market returns into w_t
'Special' series on slide 7 is not defined

relations.why: both size positions by expected return over variance

relations.other_idea: multiple-testing adjustments for backtests (Holm, deflated Sharpe)
relations.why: Bonferroni on CERT p-values addresses the same data-mining risk

relations.other_idea: Sharpe ratio / t-stat based strategy evaluation
relations.why: CERT replaces the t-test where tails and dependence make t unreliable
(reader) the Bob Fund is a stylised short-tail-risk strategy with smooth returns and rare crashes

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) No market-timing input is proposed; the forward-looking content is a filter: an alpha is credible going forward only if compounded market-neutral returns exceeded m/alpha-level (m = number of candidates) in-sample (step 6-7), and the size of any holding should follow (mu - rf)/sigma^2 shrunk for estimation error (step 3). The filter stops being reliable if beta drifts over time, if the candidate count is understated, or if the search horizon is too short to reach the threshold.
reader_inferences: (reader) For the Global Macro Book, the CERT test is a usable non-parametric check on strategy alpha: compound the residual (beta-hedged) returns and require max cumulative value above m/0.05.
(reader) The Bob Fund maps onto short-volatility or carry strategies whose smooth returns hide crash risk; Sharpe-based tests overstate their significance.
(reader) Bob's residual plot (two levels) and steady CERT path suggest a constructed series with a fixed small excess and rare jumps, but the slides do not say so.
(reader) Berkshire's CERT success may reflect known factor exposures; with a multi-factor model it might not reject.
(reader) The Kelly 1.75 figure appears to be an arithmetic slip (1.875), not a different formula.
